question: Can a bacterium intercept a nutrient-releasing source moving faster than it swims by attracting to a fast-diffusing compound while repelling from a slower one, thereby inferring a direction ahead of the lagging plume?

key_findings.claim: A single attractant gradient systematically points behind a moving source and can steer a microbe away from the lead trajectory needed for interception.
key_findings.evidence: In the point-source plume model, when the source is 20% faster than the microbe, the attractant-gradient direction differs from the straight-line optimal intercept direction by more than 60 degrees on average and more than 90 degrees at some positions. A deterministic 6-micrometer-per-second microbe fails to intercept a 9-micrometer-per-second particle despite a geometrically feasible waiting/intercept path.

anchors.section: Results: Following the gradient of an attractant is a poor strategy

key_findings.claim: Different diffusivities turn two co-emitted chemicals into a directional baseline: subtracting the slower plume from the faster plume can point ahead of the source.
key_findings.evidence: The heterogeneous MWC model combines four attractant and two repellent receptors in a response function whose gradient has a maximum in front of the moving particle. In the illustrative trajectory, attraction to a 1000-square-micrometer-per-second nutrient plus repulsion from a 250-square-micrometer-per-second nutrient produces a late downward turn and a successful intercept where pure attraction fails.

anchors.section: Adding repulsion from a slow-diffusing nutrient, Figure 2

key_findings.claim: Under deterministic gradient-following, the differential strategy substantially enlarges the modeled catchment area across a broad parameter sweep.
key_findings.evidence: For a 10-micrometer-radius particle moving at 9 micrometers per second, the intercept kernel grows from 7,500 to 22,000 square micrometers, a 183% increase. Across radii 1-100 micrometers and source speeds 1-10 times microbe speed, the mean increase is 117%, with more than six-fold gains for small sources moving about twice as fast as the microbe.

anchors.section: A differential strategy robustly increases likelihood

key_findings.claim: The qualitative benefit survives release-rate, receptor-ratio, fluid-flow, and motility variations, but its realistic stochastic effect is much smaller than the six-fold headline.
key_findings.evidence: Averaging log-uniform repellent/attractant release ratios from 0.1 to 10 gives an 88% deterministic kernel increase, and the strategy is beneficial for diffusivity ratios above about 1.3 with tuned receptor composition. Explicit E. coli-like run-and-tumble simulations improve probabilistic kernels by 5-16%; marine run-and-reverse simulations improve them by about 6%. With finite-element plumes and flow, some small-particle cases reach 254%, while large particles can worsen.

anchors.section: Robustness to release rate and receptor composition

key_findings.claim: Published amino-acid measurements are consistent with the required sign-diffusivity relationship, but this is a post hoc correlation rather than evidence that E. coli evolved or deploys the interception strategy.
key_findings.evidence: Combining prior MG1655 chemotaxis labels with five historical diffusion-coefficient sources, all eight labeled attractants lie above 790 square micrometers per second in every measurement and all seven repellents lie below that cutoff except two entries. The paper performs no moving-source experiment, receptor perturbation, or evolutionary comparison, and acknowledges nutrient utility and growth inhibition as alternative explanations.

anchors.section: E. coli is attracted to fast-diffusing amino acids, Figure 4

method.core_idea: Treat unequal molecular diffusivities as two delayed views of a moving emitter and use opposite chemotactic signs to construct a spatial derivative that leads the source rather than following its trailing plume.
method.mechanism: Analytic or finite-element advection-diffusion plumes feed a heterogeneous Monod-Wyman-Changeux receptor response. Deterministic gradient ascent and stochastic run-and-tumble/run-and-reverse agents are propagated around a sinking sphere; strategies are compared using the cross-sectional area of initial positions leading to interception.
assumptions: The source moves at constant velocity and releases each nutrient at a constant rate.
A heterogeneous receptor cluster combines attractant and repellent signals according to the simplified MWC response function.
The cross-sectional intercept kernel is proportional to ecological encounter probability because relevant initial positions are sampled uniformly.
Amino-acid diffusion coefficients measured in bulk solution approximate plume diffusivities in the relevant environment.
The selected E. coli or marine motility parameters and receptor-affinity normalization represent the organisms being generalized about.
Catching the source is a meaningful fitness proxy even when differential trajectories take longer in cases both strategies succeed.

techniques.role: Uses the angular difference between fast and slow chemical plumes to infer source motion direction.
Combines attractive and repulsive ligand binding into a differentiable chemotactic response field.
Measures the cross-sectional set of initial positions from which a simulated microbe contacts the source.
Replaces deterministic drift with run-and-tumble or run-and-reverse trajectories.
Tests point-source and no-flow simplifications against advective diffusion and particle hydrodynamics.
Relates historical amino-acid diffusivity measurements to prior E. coli attraction/repulsion labels.

evaluations.setting: Deterministic E. coli-inspired agent around a 10-micrometer sphere moving at 9 micrometers per second, with fast attractant and slow repellent emitted at 1 fmol/s.
evaluations.metric: Intercept success and intercept-kernel cross-sectional area.
evaluations.result: Differential chemotaxis catches the source and raises the kernel by 183% relative to pure attraction.
evaluations.baseline: MWC-like response to only the fast-diffusing attractant.

evaluations.setting: Sweeps over particle radius, relative speed, release-rate ratio, diffusivity ratio, density, and attractant/repellent receptor composition.
evaluations.metric: Relative change in deterministic intercept kernel and geometric-mean kernel.
evaluations.result: Average gains remain positive over the chosen broad priors, including 88% over 0.1-10x repellent release; some regions are strongly harmful and benefit requires a sufficient diffusivity ratio and receptor balance.
evaluations.baseline: Pure attraction for the same source and microbe.

evaluations.setting: E. coli-like stochastic run-and-tumble models at three noise levels and marine run-and-reverse models with finite-element plumes and source-induced flow.
evaluations.result: Differential response improves E. coli-like kernels by 5-16% and the marine case by roughly 6%, much less than deterministic gains but still positive.
evaluations.baseline: Matched stochastic motility with attractant-only response.

evaluations.setting: Seven attractant and eight repellent/conditional amino-acid labels from prior MG1655 experiments paired with diffusion coefficients from five literature sources.
evaluations.metric: Separation of chemotactic sign by diffusion coefficient.
evaluations.result: A roughly 790-square-micrometer-per-second threshold separates every attractant measurement from all but two repellent measurements.
evaluations.baseline: No mechanistic/evolutionary null model; visual cross-study association only.

limitations: The paper is principally a theoretical and simulation study; no bacterium is tested against a moving source emitting the proposed pair of chemicals.
The strongest six-fold result comes from deterministic perfect gradient following, whereas explicit stochastic models yield only 5-16% and about 6% gains.
Receptor numbers, affinities, and signal signs are simplified and partly chosen near modeled optima; actual co-clustering and pathway integration for the relevant amino acids are not measured.

The amino-acid association is post hoc, has few compounds, mixed historical measurement conditions, categorical ambiguities, and confounds diffusivity with molecular size, metabolism, toxicity, and receptor identity.
Constant straight source motion and steady emission omit tumbling prey, intermittent exudation, chemical consumption, turbulence, degradation, and competing sources.
A uniform initial-position intercept kernel is not a demonstrated ecological encounter distribution or direct fitness measure.
Where both strategies intercept, the differential path is usually slower, so success-area gains may trade against uptake duration or competition.
failure_modes: The repellent release rate overwhelms attraction and drives the microbe away; some swept regions show nearly ten-fold kernel decreases.
Attractant and repellent diffusivities are too similar to provide a usable angular baseline.
Motility noise erases the precise late turn needed to lead the source.
Large-particle hydrodynamic advection dominates receptor-driven steering and can reverse the comparative gain.
Nutrient uptake reshapes one plume faster than the other, invalidating the fixed analytical response field.
Natural receptor architecture cannot independently tune the two weights or binds a compound with concentration-dependent sign.
reusable_insights: Two signals with different propagation speeds can encode source velocity even when neither instantaneous gradient points toward the future source location.
Navigation strategies should be scored under realistic stochastic kinematics; deterministic gradient ascent can dramatically overstate effect size.
Robustness sweeps should state the prior over environmental parameters because an average benefit can depend on how source sizes and release ratios are weighted.
A simple orthogonal attractant/repellent gradient assay is a decisive first test of whether cells can vectorially combine nonparallel cues.
Cross-study ecological correlations are best treated as hypothesis generation until receptor perturbations and behavioral interventions establish causality.
open_questions: Do E. coli or marine isolates actually lead a moving dual-nutrient source, and is performance lost when the repellent receptor is deleted?
Can receptor expression evolve toward the predicted square-root relationship with diffusivity ratio under moving-source selection?
How does nutrient consumption, turbulent intermittency, source acceleration, or multiple emitters change the information available from differential diffusion?
Is catch probability, integrated nutrient exposure, time-to-contact, or post-contact retention the correct fitness objective?
Can the strategy be engineered in synthetic chemotaxis circuits or microrobots as a general propagation-delay navigator?

competitive_landscape.title: Encounter rates between bacteria and small sinking particles
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest prior mechanistic treatment of bacterial encounters with moving marine particles, including translational and rotational hydrodynamics.
competitive_landscape.difference: Słomka et al. quantify stochastic encounter rates and fluid-mediated trajectories for single-cue chemotaxis; the target imports their flow model but adds differential attractant/repellent steering to lead the particle.

competitive_landscape.title: Bacteria push the limits of chemotactic precision to navigate dynamic chemical gradients
competitive_landscape.relationship: Experimental and theoretical benchmark for microbial navigation of realistic, time-evolving dissolved-organic-matter hotspots under molecule-counting noise.
competitive_landscape.difference: Brumley et al. measure detection limits and aggregation around diffusing pulses; the target assumes sensed gradients and asks whether differential diffusion can encode a moving emitter's future position.

competitive_landscape.title: A Mathematical Description of Bacterial Chemotaxis in Response to Two Stimuli
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct mathematical predecessor for combining multiple simultaneous chemoeffector signals in E. coli-like chemotaxis.
competitive_landscape.difference: Park and Aminzare develop receptor-level responses and population drift for two stimuli; the target adapts that framework to nonparallel plumes and evaluates moving-source interception.

competitive_landscape.title: Collective responses of bacteria to a local source of conflicting effectors
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct experimental evidence for bacteria exposed to one source emitting both nutrient attractants and pH/indole repellents.
competitive_landscape.difference: Livne et al. observe population redistribution and a proximal repellent/distal attractant balance around a stationary source; the target predicts vectorial integration of nonparallel gradients around a moving source.

competitive_landscape.title: Migration and accumulation of bacteria with chemotaxis and chemokinesis
competitive_landscape.relationship: Alternative navigation mechanism for dynamic finite-size nutrient sources that changes swimming speed in addition to chemotactic bias.
competitive_landscape.difference: Jakuszeit et al. show chemokinesis can reduce measurement bias in decaying gradients; the target holds the motility response form fixed and extracts directional information from two molecular diffusivities.

competitive_landscape.title: An atlas of metabolites driving chemotaxis in prokaryotes
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current broad evidence base cataloging attractants and repellents, their thresholds, taxa, and alternative ecological interpretations.
competitive_landscape.difference: The atlas finds repulsion understudied and often but not always tied to harmfulness, emphasizing assay and taxonomic confounds; the target proposes differential diffusion as a specific adaptive explanation from a small E. coli amino-acid subset.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference after checking moving-particle hydrodynamics, dynamic-gradient sensing, two-stimulus models, conflicting-effector experiments, chemokinesis, and the current metabolite atlas: the distinctive idea is to use unequal diffusion delays with opposite chemotactic signs as a motion-parallax signal that points ahead of a source. Prior work covers all major components separately, but not this particular interception construction. The simulation evidence is thoughtful and well stress-tested; the biological/evolutionary claim remains a compelling hypothesis until a dual-cue moving-source experiment and receptor perturbation are performed.
reviewer_notes: Read all 24 extracted pages, including stochastic and finite-element supplementary analyses and full methods. This review separates the deterministic headline from smaller stochastic effects and treats the amino-acid pattern as correlational. Competitor records were checked against primary arXiv and Nature pages on 2026-08-23.
